content: Betalains are a group of pigments derived from indole, which are responsible for red and yellow coloration in plants belonging to the order Caryophyllales. These pigments are most prominently observed in the petals of flowers but can also be found in the fruits, leaves, stems, and roots of plants that produce them. The term betalain originates from the Latin name of the common beet, Beta vulgaris, as betalains were first extracted from this plant. The deep red coloration seen in beets, bougainvillea, amaranth, and various cacti is due to the presence of betalain pigments. The specific hues of red to purple produced by betalains are unique and differ from the coloration caused by anthocyanin pigments, which are more commonly found in plants. Betalains can be present in any part of the plant, including flowers, fruits, leaves, stems, and roots. Betalains are categorized into two main types: Betacyanins, which produce reddish to violet pigments. Betaxanthins, which are responsible for yellow to orange pigmentation. The biological role of betalains in plants remains uncertain, but preliminary evidence suggests they may possess antifungal properties. Initially, betalains were thought to be related to anthocyanins, as both are water-soluble pigments located in the vacuoles of plant cells. However, betalains are structurally and chemically distinct from anthocyanins. For instance, betalains contain nitrogen, whereas anthocyanins do not. Betalains are aromatic indole derivatives synthesized from the amino acid tyrosine. They are not chemically related to anthocyanins and are not classified as flavonoids. Each betalain molecule is a glycoside, consisting of a sugar molecule and a colored component. Their synthesis is light-dependent. The most extensively studied betalain is betanin, also known as beetroot red, as it can be extracted from red beet roots. Betanin is a glycoside that hydrolyzes into glucose and betanidin. It is widely used as a natural food coloring agent, with its color being sensitive to pH changes. Other betalains found in beets include isobetanin, probetanin, and neobetanin. Additional important betacyanins include amaranthine and isoamaranthine, which have been isolated from species of Amaranthus. Betalains are exclusively found in plants of the order Caryophyllales and some Basidiomycota fungi (mushrooms). In plants, betalains sometimes coexist with anthoxanthins (yellow to orange flavonoids) but never occur in species that produce anthocyanins. Within the Caryophyllales, most members produce betalains and lack anthocyanins. However, two families within this order, Caryophyllaceae (the carnation family) and Molluginaceae, produce anthocyanins instead of betalains. The restricted distribution of betalains among plants is considered a synapomorphy (a shared derived trait) for the Caryophyllales, although their production has been lost in these two families. Recently, betalain-like compounds have been identified in carnivorous plants, such as Drosera (sundew) and Nepenthes, which were not previously associated with the Caryophyllales but have been reclassified into this order under the APG II system. Betanin, a betalain pigment, is commercially utilized as a natural food dye. In some individuals, it can cause beeturia, a condition characterized by red-colored urine and feces due to the inability to metabolize the pigment. The food industry has shown increasing interest in betalains because they have been identified as natural antioxidants, which may confer health benefits to humans. Additionally, the Hopi Amerindians historically used the red flowers of the Hopi Red Dye amaranth as a source of a deep red dye.
